\chapter{Please, Sorry, and Welcome}
\label{ch:bn-please-sorry-welcome}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say please and sorry in Bengali, excuse myself politely, and welcome someone with a word that carries the same 'hither' prefix already met on the verb for coming.}

The chapter closes on \bn{স্বাগতম}, 'welcome', literally 'a good coming': su-, 'good' (PIE h1su-, cousin of Greek eu-), fused by ordinary sandhi onto āgata, 'arrived', which opens with the same ā- 'hither' prefix already met on āsā, this time riding √gam, PIE g\textsuperscript{w}em-, the secure direct ancestor of English come. The reader gives all four new words of the chapter — doya kore, dukkhito, maf korben, shbagotom — closing the two courtesy concepts, please and sorry, this book had never taught, and a third greeting concept, welcome.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[doya kore]{\bn{দয়া} \bn{করে} (doya kore) — \textquotedblleft{}please,\textquotedblright{} a kindness done}

\label{lesson:BN-C13-doya-kore}



\begin{quote}
The heart word closed the last chapter. A new one opens on a feeling that starts in the same place — and a word this book has never taught you before now.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{দয়া} \bn{করে}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{দয়া} \bn{করে}} — \emph{doya kore} — \textbf{please}
\end{quote}

\bn{দয়া} \bn{করে} \bn{বসুন} (\emph{doya kore bôshun}) — please, sit.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{দয়া}} is \textbf{\bn{দ}} (\emph{dô}) plus \textbf{\bn{য়}} (the glide already met inside \bn{হৃদয়}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}): \emph{doyā}. \textbf{\bn{করে}} is \textbf{\bn{ক}} (\emph{kô}) plus \textbf{\bn{র}} (\emph{r}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ে}} (\emph{e}): \emph{kôre}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{দয়া}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{দয়া}} (\emph{dayā}), \textquotedblleft{}compassion, pity.\textquotedblright{} Most Indo-Europeanists trace its root back to PIE \textbf{*deh\textsubscript{2}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to divide, to apportion\textquotedblright{} — the same root proposed for Greek \emph{daíomai}, \textquotedblleft{}to divide,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{dêmos}, \textquotedblleft{}a portion of land, the people,\textquotedblright{} which English holds without inheriting it directly: \textbf{democracy}, \textbf{epidemic}, \textbf{demographic}. If the comparison is right, compassion and sharing are the same idea at the root — you feel \bn{দয়া} for someone by dividing your own good fortune with them, the warmth this book already located in \textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}}, the heart.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \bn{করা} wears a new outfit}]
Noun plus \bn{করা} already builds a verb — \bn{কাজ} \bn{করা}, \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}; \bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} \bn{করা}, \textquotedblleft{}to ask.\textquotedblright{} Here \bn{করা} takes a different shape, \textbf{\bn{করে}}, \textquotedblleft{}having done\textquotedblright{}: not a full sentence on its own, but a piece that leans on the next word.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape of \bn{করা}} & \textbf{job} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
a finite ending (\bn{করি}, \bn{করে}, \bn{করেন}…) & states an action & \bn{আমি} \bn{কাজ} \bn{করি} — I work \\
\textbf{\bn{করে}}, unchanged & \textquotedblleft{}having done,\textquotedblright{} leaning forward & \textbf{\bn{দয়া} \bn{করে} \bn{বসুন}} — please, sit \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\bn{দয়া} \bn{করে} literally says \textquotedblleft{}having done a kindness, {[}now do this{]}\textquotedblright{} — the kindness is named, then the actual request follows.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}doya\textquotedblright{} — compassion, then \textquotedblleft{}kore\textquotedblright{} — having done
  \item \textquotedblleft{}doya kore bôshun\textquotedblright{} — please, sit
  \item the family this word joins — \textquotedblleft{}kāj kôrā … jijñāsā kôrā … doya kore\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \bn{দয়া} \bn{করে} mean literally, piece by piece? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Having done a kindness\textquotedblright{}} — \bn{দয়া} \textquotedblleft{}compassion\textquotedblright{} + \bn{করে} \textquotedblleft{}having done.\textquotedblright{}) Is \bn{করে} here a full sentence by itself? (\textbf{No} — it leans forward onto the request that follows it.) One quick reach back: what root does \bn{দয়া} share with a very old disputed argument about \textbf{democracy}? (\textbf{PIE deh\textsubscript{2}-, \textquotedblleft{}to divide\textquotedblright{}} — the same proposed root behind Greek \emph{dêmos}, and behind the warmth \textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}}, the heart, already carries — two lessons after \bn{নাক}, the nose, which shares none of it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dukkhito]{\bn{দুঃখিত} (dukkhito) — \textquotedblleft{}sorry,\textquotedblright{} and a prefix that reaches Greek}

\label{lesson:BN-C13-dukkhito}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson's kindness gets a request said politely. This lesson is what you say when the kindness came too late.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{দুঃখিত}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{দুঃখিত}} — \emph{dukkhito} — \textbf{sorry}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{দুঃখিত} (\emph{āmi dukkhito}) — I'm sorry.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{দুঃখিত}} is \textbf{\bn{দ}} (\emph{dô}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ু}} (\emph{u}), then \textbf{\bn{ঃ}} — a new mark, the \textbf{visarga}, two small stacked dots that add a light breath after the vowel — then \textbf{\bn{খ}} (\emph{kh}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ি}} (\emph{i}), then \textbf{\bn{ত}} (\emph{t}, silent at the end). Spelled \emph{duḥkhita}, said \emph{dukkhito}: the breath mark softens toward the consonant that follows it rather than staying a separate sound.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{দুঃখিত}} is built on Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{দুঃখ}} (\emph{duḥkha}), \textquotedblleft{}sorrow, suffering\textquotedblright{} — the word Buddhism made famous as \emph{dukkha}. Take it apart and one half is certain: \textbf{\bn{দুঃ}/\bn{দুস্}} (\emph{dus-}) means \textquotedblleft{}bad, difficult,\textquotedblright{} from PIE \textbf{*dus-}, the very prefix inside Greek \textbf{dys-}: \textbf{dystopia}, \textbf{dysfunctional}. The other half, \textbf{\bn{খ}} (\emph{kha}), is where the certainty ends. Sanskrit's own grammatical tradition explains it as \textquotedblleft{}an axle-hole\textquotedblright{} — a \emph{duḥkha} journey is a \textbf{bad axle-hole}, a rough ride, set against \textbf{\bn{সুখ}} (\emph{sukha}), \textquotedblleft{}a good axle-hole,\textquotedblright{} comfort. It is a vivid story, and it is repeated everywhere. It is also, by the account of modern Sanskritists including Mayrhofer, not a story to trust: the axle-hole reading may be a later folk explanation grafted onto a word whose real root is lost. \bn{দুঃ}'s cousin is real; \bn{খ}'s is a story, reported and not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dukkhito\textquotedblright{} — sorry
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmi dukkhito\textquotedblright{} — I'm sorry
  \item the secure half and its Greek cousin — \textquotedblleft{}dus- … dystopia\textquotedblright{}
  \item last lesson's request again — \textquotedblleft{}doya kore bôshun\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I'm sorry\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{দুঃখিত}.}) Which half of \bn{দুঃখ} is a secure PIE prefix, and which English word shares it? (\textbf{\bn{দুঃ}/dus-, \textquotedblleft{}bad\textquotedblright{}} — \textbf{dystopia}, by way of Greek \emph{dys-}.) Is the \textquotedblleft{}bad axle-hole\textquotedblright{} story of \bn{খ} settled fact? (\textbf{No} — a repeated tradition, treated with real skepticism by modern Sanskritists.) Sorrow, like compassion, can weigh somewhere specific — where? (\textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}}, the heart.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maf korben]{\bn{মাফ} \bn{করবেন} (maf korben) — \textquotedblleft{}excuse me,\textquotedblright{} borrowed and softened}

\label{lesson:BN-C13-maf-korben}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson's word for \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} was a native Sanskrit word. This one is a loanword — the very same loanword Hindi uses in its own \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} phrase — and it softens a request in a way you have not met yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{মাফ} \bn{করবেন}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{মাফ} \bn{করবেন}} — \emph{maf korben} — \textbf{excuse me}
\end{quote}

\bn{মাফ} \bn{করবেন}, \bn{একটু} \bn{জায়গা} \bn{দেবেন}? (\emph{maf korben, êktu jāygā debên?}) — excuse me, could you make a little room?

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{মাফ}} is \textbf{\bn{ম}} (\emph{mô}) with \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}) plus \textbf{\bn{ফ}} (\emph{ph}, the puffed \emph{p}). Notice what is missing: Hindi marks this same borrowed sound with a small dot under its own letter for \emph{pha}, a \emph{nuqtā}, to write a dedicated letter for \emph{f}. Bengali's script has no such mark at all — \textbf{\bn{ফ}} alone serves for both the native puffed \emph{p} and this borrowed \emph{f}, and only habit tells a reader which one a given word means.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{মাফ}} is not Bengali, and not Sanskrit: it is borrowed, by way of Persian, from Arabic \emph{\textbf{'afw}}, \textquotedblleft{}to pardon, to wipe a wrong away.\textquotedblright{} Hindi borrowed the identical word for the identical job. Bengali also keeps a formal, Sanskritic cousin for the same idea, \textbf{\bn{ক্ষমা} \bn{করবেন}}, from \textbf{\bn{ক্ষমা}} (\emph{kṣamā}), \textquotedblleft{}patience, forbearance\textquotedblright{} — the everyday loan and the bookish native word side by side, the same split Hindi keeps.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the future, asked to be gentle}]
The tea-offering pattern you already own reuses a \textbf{present} verb — \bn{আপনি} \bn{খান} — to make a request. \textbf{\bn{করবেন}} does the same job with a different tense: it is the plain \textbf{future}, \textquotedblleft{}you will do,\textquotedblright{} not a command at all by its grammar, and yet its job here is exactly a request — a third shape for \bn{করা}, beside last lesson's participle \textbf{\bn{করে}}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{tense used} & \textbf{what it does} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
present habitual & states, and doubles as a request & \bn{আপনি} \bn{খান} — you eat / please eat \\
\textbf{future} & states, and doubles as a \emph{softer} request & \textbf{\bn{মাফ} \bn{করবেন}} — you will excuse / please excuse \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The future's distance is what buys the softness: asking rather than telling, even grammatically.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maf korben\textquotedblright{} — excuse me
  \item the two soft requests compared — \textquotedblleft{}chā khān … maf korben\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \bn{মাফ} come from? (\textbf{Arabic 'afw, \textquotedblleft{}to pardon,\textquotedblright{} by way of Persian} — the same loan Hindi's own \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} phrase uses.) What tense is \bn{করবেন}, and why does that make it gentler than a command? (\textbf{Future} — \textquotedblleft{}you will do,\textquotedblright{} asking rather than telling.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shbagotom]{\bn{স্বাগতম} (shbagotom) — \textquotedblleft{}welcome,\textquotedblright{} a good arrival}

\label{lesson:BN-C13-sbagotom}



\begin{quote}
This chapter has taught what to say after a mistake. It closes on what to say before anything goes wrong at all — a word built on the same \textquotedblleft{}hither\textquotedblright{} you have carried since the verb for \textbf{coming}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{স্বাগতম}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{স্বাগতম}} — \emph{shbagotom} — \textbf{welcome}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমাদের} \bn{বাড়িতে} \bn{স্বাগতম} (\emph{āmāder bāṛite shbagotom}) — welcome to our house.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{স্বাগতম}} is \textbf{\bn{স্ব}} (a conjunct, \bn{স} joined straight to \bn{ব} with no vowel between — \emph{sbô}, tilted by the same \emph{s$\to$sh} habit every Sanskrit word in this book has shown) plus \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}), then \textbf{\bn{গ}} (\emph{gô}), \textbf{\bn{ত}} (\emph{tô}), and \textbf{\bn{ম}} (\emph{mô}, keeping its own inherent vowel at the very end): \emph{shbā-go-to-m}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{স্বাগতম}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{স্বাগতম}} (\emph{svāgatam}), built from two pieces fused together. The second piece, \textbf{\bn{আগত}} (\emph{āgata}), \textquotedblleft{}arrived, come,\textquotedblright{} opens with the very same \textbf{\bn{আ}-}, \textquotedblleft{}hither,\textquotedblright{} that \bn{আসা}'s own lesson already named — except here it rides a different verb, \textbf{√\bn{গম্}} (\emph{√gam}, \textquotedblleft{}to go, to come\textquotedblright{}), not \bn{আসা}'s own unsettled stem. \textbf{√gam} is PIE \textbf{*g\textsuperscript{w}em-}, and this root is about as secure as roots get: it is the direct ancestor of English \textbf{come}, and, by way of Latin \textbf{venīre}, of \textbf{advent} and \textbf{convene} too. The first piece, \textbf{\bn{সু}-} (\emph{su-}, \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}), loses its vowel to the glide \textbf{\bn{ব}} when the next syllable also opens with a vowel — ordinary Sanskrit sandhi, the same trade \textbf{\bn{সু}-} plus \textbf{\bn{আগত}} makes every time: \emph{svāgata}. \bn{সু}- is PIE \textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}su-}, cousin of Greek \textbf{eu-}, the \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} inside \textbf{eulogy} and \textbf{euphoria}. Put the pieces back together: \bn{স্বাগতম} is, literally, \textquotedblleft{}a good coming.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}shbagotom\textquotedblright{} — welcome
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmāder bāṛite shbagotom\textquotedblright{} — welcome to our house
  \item the shared prefix — \textquotedblleft{}ā-, hither\textquotedblright{} — on āsā, then on āgata
  \item the two secure cousins — \textquotedblleft{}gam … come\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}su- … eu-\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}welcome\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{স্বাগতম}.}) What does \bn{স্বাগতম} mean, piece by piece? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Good\textquotedblright{} plus \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{} — a good arrival.}) Which prefix does it share with \bn{আসা}, and on a different verb this time? (\textbf{\bn{আ}-, \textquotedblleft{}hither\textquotedblright{}} — on √gam here, not \bn{আসা}'s own uncertain stem.) Run this chapter's three other new words back: a kindness done, a word for sorrow, and a borrowed pardon. (\textbf{\bn{দয়া} \bn{করে}, \bn{দুঃখিত}, \bn{মাফ} \bn{করবেন}.}) One more reach: what tense softened that pardon into a request? (\textbf{Future} — \bn{করবেন}, \textquotedblleft{}you will do.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
